line1_base: Objects placed flat with their center of gravity within the effective base of support are stable by default.
Do not predict dramatic or chain-reaction collapses in everyday scenes unless there is clearly insufficient physical support, a steep incline, or a significant external force.
Perturbations where the agent's mass is less than 1% of the structure's mass (e.g., a bird landing, a raindrop) have no significant effect.
Perturbations where the agent's mass is greater than 10% of the structure's mass (e.g., a person climbing a light ladder) cause significant displacement or tipping.
Forces applied above an object's center of gravity tend to cause tipping, while forces applied below tend to cause sliding.

Precision-balanced structures (e.g., card houses, objects balanced on a point) are extremely vulnerable to minor vibrations, whereas anchored or heavy structures (e.g., lamp posts, trees, wall-mounted TVs) are unaffected by everyday light impacts.
When determining the 'least stable' object, assess only the geometric ratio of the base of support relative to the height. Fragility does not equal instability.

On inclines, objects with curved contact surfaces (spheres, sideways cylinders) will roll at minor tilts of 1-2 degrees. Objects with flat bases rely on friction and typically remain stationary up to 5-15 degrees.
When an object is removed from an arrangement, only the objects that directly depend on it for support will fall. Objects with independent support remain unaffected.

When a person sits or jumps on heavy furniture (e.g., beds, sofas, benches), the furniture itself remains stable. Only loose, lightweight items on the surface (e.g., pillows, loose papers, unanchored blankets) will bounce or be displaced.
Humans possess active muscle reflexes to recover balance. They will not fall uncontrollably from minor obstacles or slight forces unless the environment is extremely steep or slippery.

Visibility must always be evaluated from the queried observer's viewpoint, not from the camera's viewpoint. To decide what a seated person or a standing teacher can see, mentally reposition the viewpoint to that person's eye location and facing direction before checking line-of-sight.

An object that is present in the scene may still be not visible, only partially visible, or not clearly readable from a different viewpoint. Presence in the image does not guarantee visibility from every position within the scene.

Gaze direction of a person is primarily determined by head and torso orientation, not by proximity on the grid. The nearest object is not necessarily the one being looked at; the object aligned with the person's forward-facing axis is.

Occlusion is viewpoint-dependent and asymmetric: a smaller foreground object can partially hide a larger background object when they overlap along the viewing ray from the observer. Two objects side by side in the image plane do not occlude each other unless their projected extents actually overlap from the relevant viewpoint.

For questions about whether text on a sign, shop name, or board is clearly readable, consider the observer's distance, angle of incidence, and whether foreground clutter or structural elements intervene. A sign can be physically present yet unreadable from an oblique seated position.

Furniture such as benches, sofas, desks, and stadium seating imposes a natural facing direction. A person sitting on a bench typically faces the open or focal side. Use this prior to infer what they can or cannot see.

When counting fully visible people, an individual is fully visible only if no part of their body is materially clipped by the image boundary or occluded by another object. Partially cropped or overlapping figures should not be counted as fully visible.

Objects placed behind other objects of the same semantic category (e.g., a large vase behind a smaller vase) can still be partially hidden. Occlusion depends on spatial overlap in projection, not on category membership.

The image is the observation; the scene graph is an estimated, potentially incomplete description. A named node does not prove that the object exists or has the asserted identity. Nothing, none, not applicable, and statements about depth or possibility are answer meanings, not physical objects with measurable locations.

Several mutually exclusive names assigned to the exact same image point do not provide independent evidence for those names. Extremely large repeated depths can be saturation or estimation failure, not evidence that all targets occupy the same distant plane. Verify such cases with visible contours and layout rather than breaking ties by listed order.

A scene-graph anchor is one sampled image point, not an object's full footprint, outline or extent. Depth at a transparent, reflective, thin or occluded point may belong to another surface. Do not let an implausible numeric ordering overrule clear overlap or contact boundaries. Keep valid geometry when it agrees with the image; do not discard every number merely because one estimate is bad.

A reference missing from the graph must be located in the image. Do not invent its coordinates, give it the depth of an unrelated named node, or pretend that the listed candidate objects exhaust the scene.

For image left/right/top/bottom/corners use image points and visible extent: pixel x increases rightward and pixel y increases downward. Larger y means lower in the picture. Camera X/Y values include perspective scaling and cannot replace pixel ordering when objects are at different depths. For an ordinal corner position, establish the full order including the first item before selecting the second.

Nearest to a named object means distance from that object, not nearest to the camera. If consistent 3D coordinates exist for both reference and candidate, compare squared distance (X-Xref)^2+(Y-Yref)^2+(Z-Zref)^2. A small Z alone means nearer to the camera; a small absolute Z difference alone only means similar camera depth. Neither proves that two laterally separated objects are close.

For distance to an extended road, doorway or furniture surface, locate the relevant boundary or part in the image. The camera is not automatically on that road or at that reference. Do not substitute camera distance when the actual reference is absent from the graph.

Appearance alignment is not facing direction. Compare compatible landmarks or positions on both axes. A substantial vertical offset together with a horizontal offset gives diagonal image alignment. Several objects may lie approximately along an image row even if noisy camera depths differ; use 3D collinearity only when the question asks physical ground-plane alignment.

A collection can include both horizontal rows and vertical columns. One graph node representing cabinets cannot establish the arrangement of the individual doors. Side by side means neighboring on the same supporting layer; it does not require a perfectly straight row or identical orientation.

In front in camera depth differs from layered in front of or obscuring another object. Occlusion requires projected overlap and interrupted target contours as well as front-to-back ordering. A floor item nearer to the camera but below and separated from a bucket does not cover the bucket. None can be correct for an occlusion question despite nearer objects elsewhere in the image.

Directly behind asks for the background immediately aligned with the target's visible region or specified rear direction. Do not choose the first candidate with greater Z or the object farthest away in the whole scene. Inspect the local background surface, not all distant objects indiscriminately. A vehicle carrying people is a distinct whole from an individual person seated in it.

Apply all spatial clauses to the same candidate: behind one reference and in front of another is an intersection of constraints, not permission to choose whichever single relation matches. Resolve which instance of repeated trees, people or animals supplies each reference. A nearer tree at the frame edge does not stand for every tree in the background.

Behind a person may refer to the side behind the person's body, while behind in the image refers to camera depth. Obstructing a person's view requires that person's eye-to-target line; hiding the person from the camera requires camera-to-person overlap. State the interpretation supported by the wording and image rather than substitute minimum Z for either relation.

For relations inside a reflected scene, compare depicted objects inside that scene. The mirror holding the image is not automatically between every pair of reflected landmarks. Likewise a picture displayed on a screen does not put the depicted landscape at the physical depth of the screen.

Filter candidates by visible attributes before ranking: paper can be white even when not called white in the node name. Distinguish the color of a visible cup, cover or handle from a mistaken graph label by comparing it with neighboring colors. Object identity and color are hypotheses to verify, not facts guaranteed by a node name.

When a compound option names two parts of a visible integrated appliance, verify both parts against the requested region. A cooker can have a stove top and oven below the same hood. Do not stop after recognizing the most salient component, but do not choose a compound answer unless every named component satisfies the question.

For ordinal proximity or depth, identify the reference and sort all eligible candidates using the requested relation; do not mix a horizontal rank with a depth rank. Exclude the reference itself when counting other objects or objects strictly between endpoints. For a row of books, distinguish intervening book count from positional separation; use visible spine boundaries and the wording, not invented titles or hypothetical positions.

Trace a person's approach corridor or hand-reach region to the actual target. Objects elsewhere in the photograph do not automatically require removal. Distinguish visual overlap from an obstruction to physical access. A seated person may need clearance beside a chair before walking, but a chair is not a blocker just because it is named in the graph.

For falling objects, inspect the vertical sweep and the nearest intervening surface. Furniture below can be the first contact before the floor; the relative depths of single sampled centers do not by themselves exclude an overlap of extended objects. A later bounce needs a plausible contact and motion, not a universal rule that every falling frame bounces.

Identify the target and every named reference before ranking candidates. Nearest or second-farthest from a named object is not nearest or farthest from the camera. With consistent 3D coordinates for both objects, compare (X-Xref)^2+(Y-Yref)^2+(Z-Zref)^2. Comparing only Z or absolute Z differences ignores lateral and vertical separation. If the reference is absent from the graph, locate it in the image; do not invent its coordinates.

For between A and B, inspect the actual region separating those references and test this constraint first. Then apply frontmost or another requested rank to the eligible objects. A nearer object outside that region does not satisfy between. Below A differs from between two side-by-side landmarks.

Image-plane x grows rightward and y grows downward. Judge image center using both coordinates and the actual frame dimensions, not only the horizontal midpoint. For a head, brush head, handle, pot or edge, locate the requested part rather than use the sampled point of the whole body or shaft. A named group has extent that one point cannot describe.

Compare each eligible candidate before choosing an ordinal rank; do not stop after the first node in the graph. Node names and colors can be mistaken. Missing alternatives are not automatically irrelevant, and partly visible objects still count when their identity is supported.

A lower camera depth is not sufficient to hide another object. Occlusion needs overlapping image regions and an interrupted rear contour. Verify which shelf or local region each item occupies. Small depth differences between adjacent surfaces may be estimation noise; a visible front contour is stronger evidence than a slightly reversed estimated ordering.

An object can cover portions of multiple objects at once; inspect its whole silhouette and each option. A camera pictured as a physical object can block what is behind its body regardless of where its lens points. Do not confuse an object's field of view with the photograph's occlusion of other items. Check every part of a compound option.

Standing on asks for the immediate contact support, not merely the large surface underneath the entire arrangement. If thin layers intervene, trace the contact downward one layer at a time and count visibly distinct layers. Do not infer multiple hidden layers without visible evidence.

Alignment of several poles or trees describes the sequence of their positions, not the vertical orientation of each trunk. Upright poles can recede diagonally across an image. A row need not have identical heights or perfectly regular spacing. For pot alignment, exclude the specified plant using actual plant height, then compare the remaining pots in image x and y; similar Z does not make their image arrangement horizontal.

Treat a frame, opening or edge as a possible occluded target, not just a named standalone object. A cup can interrupt a table edge without covering another cup. Conversely an underlying puddle is not a separate object between two reflected people, and a still reflection does not prove that a splash exists.

Trace the complete route from the specified start to the destination. A node named aisle at an intermediate Z does not prove that an open walking corridor connects both endpoints. Inspect seats, railings, level changes and gaps. Furniture in a room does not itself prove blockage; only objects intersecting the needed passage count.

Use visible door state and opening geometry. An open passage beside a closed panel can provide access without opening that panel. An archway or tunnel does not by itself provide an ascent to the top of a slide; trace where the climbing connection goes. The nearest obstacle is not necessarily the fastest traversable route.

For sequences, list encountered people, occupied benches, empty benches and landmarks along the chosen approach in order. A large foreground tree off the path need not be the first encountered obstacle. At a junction follow connected crossings and corners rather than invent a diagonal crossing because the destination is across the image.

Assess obstructions separately for each requested branch or road, and check every component of a combined option. Do not swap image left/right or road segments while comparing a crowd, traffic or barriers.

Physical access depends on the operation: reaching a tabletop object uses the hand's approach and grasp region, not necessarily the floor space in front of the table. Vehicle passage needs a continuous drivable surface as well as adequate width and height; steps can prevent passage even if a doorway looks wide. For warehouse placement, count rack tiers from the bottom and inspect vacant capacity on each tier. A bay label is not a shelf level, and the lowest tier is not automatically available.

Use reflected content when the question refers to a person or road seen in a mirror. Resolve both landmarks in the same depicted scene rather than replace the relation with the mirror's physical position. Nearby mirror-surface depths do not measure distances to the reflected cars, hands or distant scenery. Do not invent a hidden seat belt, splash, flower or person from an unreliable label.

For hypothetical movement or removal, update the specified condition before answering. A distant feature viewed from close is no longer viewed at its old camera distance. Moving an object closer increases its apparent angular size while leaving its physical dimensions unchanged; the photograph alone does not prove that windows on different buildings have identical real sizes.

Removing cushions can expose a frame, rim or opening; distinguish the remaining structure from the filled cushion silhouette. A perspective ellipse does not prove an oval physical footprint, and an apparently round seat need not be a solid perfect disk. Infer the top view only as far as visible construction supports it.

Auxiliary coordinates are sampled estimates, not exact object extents or ground-truth identities. A nearby surface, thin wire, reflective lens or partly hidden object can have an incorrect estimated depth. When geometry conflicts with visible overlap or target identity, verify the relevant image region instead of repeating numerical comparisons. A label such as another coral does not make that node the requested topmost coral. Resolve the actual reference first.
